measurement.happened:
THE TRUMP-XI-PUTIN SUMMIT DOMINATES. The single biggest story of the week was the unprecedented trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi, and Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China. The three leaders issued a joint 'Declaration toward Peace,' shook hands on camera, and Putin carried his nuclear briefcase into the room. Trump called Putin 'my friend' and said they had a 'great relationship,' which infuriated Zelensky, who called Putin a 'killer' in response. The Kremlin framed the summit as a watershed moment and a deliberate snub to Europe, while European allies gathered in Berlin to coordinate a response. On substance, however, the summit produced no breakthroughs: Trump said nuclear arms limits with China and Russia would be 'very hard to achieve,' and the three-way nuclear rivalry the US now faces was described as unprecedented. Putin defended his 'Yalta' vision of a post-war order, and allies warned against a Yalta-style carve-up of Ukraine. The summit exposed what commentators called Europe's power deficit, as the big three met without European heads of state. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/18-11/20, AP 11/18-11/20, BBC 11/18-11/21, CNN 11/18-11/21, DW 11/17-11/18, FT 11/16-11/18, Bloomberg 11/18, Al Jazeera 11/16, WSJ 11/18.)

THE WAR OF BRIDGES ESCALATES. Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Crimea multiple times this week, partially collapsing a section and what Zelensky called an 'unprecedented' attack. The bridge is crucial to Russia's war logistics and its assertion of control over Crimea. Ukraine used so-called 'flying modems' to help guide the strikes. Putin vowed a 'far more painful' response and ruled out a Black Sea or energy truce. Russia hit back at Kyiv's river crossings and other infrastructure. The cleanup of the damaged bridge section is expected to take months, according to Ukraine. The 'war of bridges' became a defining image of the week, with both sides targeting the other's most symbolic infrastructure. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/19-11/20, AP 11/17-11/18, BBC 11/17-11/20, CNN 11/17, DW 11/18, FT 11/18, TV5Monde 11/17-11/18, WSJ 11/18, Bloomberg 11/17-11/21.)

RUSSIA UNLEASHES MASSIVE MISSILE AND DRONE BARRAGES ON UKRAINE. In direct retaliation for the bridge strikes and as a show of force before and after the summit, Russia launched some of its largest missile and drone attacks of the war. At least eight people were killed in one wave, a Russian 'triple-tap' attack killed a seven-year-old and an emergency worker in Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih, and dozens more were reported dead or missing. Russia targeted energy facilities, transport infrastructure, and sea vessels. Zelensky called one of the strikes 'one of the largest.' The EU accused Russia of stalling peace talks specifically to hit power plants as winter approaches. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/20, AP 11/20, BBC 11/20-11/21, CNN 11/20-11/21, DW 11/21, Al Jazeera 11/21, TV5Monde 11/21.)

A RUSSIAN MISSILE LANDS IN POLAND. During NATO military exercises near the Polish border, a Russian missile struck Polish territory. Polish Prime Minister Tusk called it a likely 'intentional provocation.' NATO officially called it a violation of Polish airspace. This was the third Polish airspace violation in the period, and it happened while Europe was holding drills nearby, raising fears of a deliberate Russian test of European nerves. (Supporting headlines: AP 11/20, BBC 11/21, Al Jazeera 11/21, DW 11/21, TV5Monde 11/21, Reuters 11/20.)

THE BALTIC SEA AND NORTHERN EUROPE BECOME A HOTSPOT. A Russian cargo ship was hit by a drone in the Gulf of Finland, with the crew evacuating. Finland detected the attack. A Russian helicopter was suspected of violating Finnish airspace around the same time. Denmark announced it had thwarted a Russian plot to assassinate a US-Ukrainian rapper on its soil, with two Danes suspected of being hired by Russian intelligence. Denmark expelled a Russian diplomat and pushed the EU to tighten travel curbs on Russians. Estonia announced it will close its land border with Russia on December 1, citing a foiled sabotage attempt on a drone factory, while Moscow decried a 'new Iron Curtain.' The Netherlands summoned the Russian ambassador after its Kyiv embassy was hit, and a mass leak of Deutsche Bank documents showed links to Russia and the Epstein case. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/20-11/21, AP 11/20, BBC 11/21, CNN 11/15, DW 11/16, FT 11/15, TV5Monde 11/16-11/21, WSJ 11/21, Al Jazeera 11/21, Bloomberg 11/16, CNBC 11/16.)

EUROPE TIGHTENS SANCTIONS AND PREPARES FOR TALKS. The EU sanctioned Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim, and she stepped down days later. The EU proposed a 45-billion-euro loan to Ukraine borrowed against the EU budget. The EU plans a visa ban for former Russian combatants. Germany's Foreign Minister Wadephul said Berlin talks send a 'strong signal to Moscow.' Europe declared itself ready for talks with Russia on ending the war. Russia, however, pushed back against the US idea of NATO-style security guarantees for Ukraine and said the EU's Kallas playing a role in talks would lead to their collapse. Kushner said Russia is 'comfortable' with NATO-like guarantees, and Russia grasped the US offer on European security to revive its own old demands. Putin proposed a second humanitarian ceasefire, which analysts questioned was a trap. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/16, 11/20-11/21, AP 11/20, BBC 11/20, CNN 11/20, DW 11/20, FT 11/15-11/16, Bloomberg 11/18, Al Jazeera 11/16, WSJ 11/15.)

RUSSIA'S ENERGY SECTOR UNDER STRAIN. Drone attacks nearly halved Russia's November oil refining capacity. More Russian regions limited fuel sales as refinery output dropped. Russia imported record volumes of petrol. Russia exported the most crude since July as drones hammered refineries. A Ukrainian drone attack hit an oil facility in Tatarstan. The Russian diesel deal under Trump struggled to reach the US market amid legal fears and criticism. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/19-11/20, AP 11/18, FT 11/18, Bloomberg 11/17, WSJ 11/15, DW 11/17.)

DOMESTIC RUSSIAN STORIES. A Russian military transport plane crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 on board. A renowned Russian ornithologist was jailed over small donations to Navalny's anti-corruption foundation. A WSJ investigation exposed sex abuse as part of the system in a Russian POW camp. The IIHF website was hacked after Russia was barred from the World Junior Hockey tournament in Canada, and Putin publicly criticized the 'disregard' for the sports ruling. Russia appealed to the IOC. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/17-11/19, AP 11/17-11/19, BBC 11/17, CNN 11/17, DW 11/21, WSJ 11/21, Al Jazeera 11/16.)

RUSSIA REPOSITIONS ITSELF AS AN ASIAN POWER. At APEC, Putin declared Russia an 'integral part of Asia-Pacific.' He pitched Russia as a place to invest. Vietnam and Russia agreed to deepen energy cooperation. Russia and Georgia resumed direct dialogue with an official meeting in Minsk. Russian nuclear-capable bombers were spotted in Vietnam before departing. Two Russian military aircraft were reported near Taiwan, the second time in a week. Japan scrambled jets after suspected Russian aircraft violated its airspace. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/19, AP 11/19, BBC 11/17, Bloomberg 11/18, Al Jazeera 11/16.)

ESPIONAGE AND INTELLIGENCE TENSIONS. The US Department of Justice charged a Russian national with targeting Palantir as a foreign agent. A US Army officer was taken into custody after being arrested in the UK for spying for Russia. The Netherlands summoned Russia's ambassador after its embassy in Kyiv was hit. A GPS signal loss in the Netherlands pointed to possible Russian sabotage. (Supporting headlines: Reuters 11/19, AP 11/17-11/18, BBC 11/18, TV5Monde 11/16.)
measurement.expected:
THE SUMMIT AFTERMATH AND EUROPEAN REACTION. Almost certain: Europe will spend the coming week digesting the Trump-Xi-Putin summit and coordinating a unified response. The Berlin meeting of Ukraine's allies already happened, and we should expect follow-up statements, press conferences, and possibly a special EU or NATO meeting to address the 'peace declaration' and the security guarantees question. Russia will likely try to split Europe by offering bilateral talks while resisting multilateral frameworks. The Kallas dispute and the NATO-style guarantees debate will dominate. Probable: The EU's 45-billion-euro Ukraine loan proposal will face its first round of parliamentary debate or member-state consultations. Possible: Denmark and Estonia will push for a formal EU response to the Baltic Sea drone attack, the rapper assassination plot, and the border closure, potentially leading to a new round of targeted sanctions or travel restrictions on Russian citizens. Unlikely: A full EU-Russia formal negotiation track will be launched this week; the groundwork is being laid, but the architecture is not ready.

WAR OF BRIDGES AND RETALIATION CYCLE. Almost certain: Russia will continue to strike Ukrainian infrastructure, particularly energy and transport, as winter approaches and the EU has accused Moscow of timing attacks to hit power plants. Ukraine will likely continue targeting Russian logistics, including the damaged Crimea bridge and other bridges. Probable: The partially collapsed section of the Kerch Bridge will be a focal point of both propaganda and military planning. Russia will either rush a temporary repair or use the damage to justify a harder military posture in the Black Sea. Possible: A new round of drone swarms against Russian refineries, given that November refining is already nearly halved. Unlikely: A full-scale ground offensive by either side this week; the pattern is aerial and drone warfare, not tank pushes.

POLAND AND NORTHERN EUROPE TENSIONS. Almost certain: Poland will demand a formal explanation or apology from Russia over the missile that landed on its territory. NATO will issue a statement, and the three prior airspace violations will be cited as a pattern. Probable: Estonia's border closure on December 1 will take effect, and Russia will respond with a diplomatic note or a minor provocation near the border. Denmark will likely follow up the rapper plot with additional intelligence briefings to EU partners. Possible: Another Russian airspace incursion over the Baltic or over Poland, as Moscow appears to be testing European reaction thresholds. Unlikely: A full NATO Article 4 consultation or a formal Article 5 discussion this week; the incidents are serious but not yet at that threshold.

ENERGY AND ECONOMIC PRESSURE. Almost certain: Russian fuel shortages will worsen in several regions as refinery output stays depressed. More regions may impose fuel rationing or price controls. Probable: Russia will accelerate imports of refined petrol and diesel. The Russian diesel deal with the US will face further legal and political friction. Possible: Oil and gas prices will remain elevated, and the optical fiber price spike caused by drone-war damage to undersea cables will be felt in telecom costs. Unlikely: A major Russian budget revision or emergency economic package this week; the damage is accumulating but not yet at a crisis threshold.

DOMESTIC RUSSIA. Probable: The Siberian plane crash (19 dead) will generate a brief wave of domestic mourning and a state investigation, followed by the usual pattern of the story fading. The ornithologist's jailing over Navalny-foundation donations will be a small but symbolically charged case for opposition circles. The POW camp sex abuse story will generate some domestic and international outrage, but Russia will likely contain the narrative. Possible: The Wildberries CEO's departure will trigger a short internal reshuffle or a statement from the company's board. Unlikely: A major domestic political event, protest, or cabinet change this week. The regime is focused on the war and the post-summit diplomacy.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES. A Russian pre-emptive strike on a Ukrainian port or naval base in the Black Sea, citing the Baltic drone attack as justification. A sudden Russian offer of a full ceasefire or a major prisoner swap to mark the post-summit 'peace' mood. A second Polish or Baltic airspace incident within the same week, escalating the NATO response. A Russian cyberattack on a European energy grid or financial system in retaliation for the Wildberries sanctions. A dramatic statement from Putin at a domestic event (e.g., a Victory Day-style speech or a Duma address) reframing the war's goals.

THINGS I WOULD NOT BET ON. A full-scale Russian ground offensive in a new sector. A major Russian nuclear test or a new ICBM launch for show. A Russian presidential election or succession announcement. A full EU-Russia trade deal or a lifting of any major sanctions. A Russian withdrawal from any occupied territory. A major Russian domestic protest or strike. A ceasefire that holds for more than 48 hours. A Russian space launch or satellite deployment as a signal. A major Russian budget deficit crisis or a rouble collapse.

Russia's massive retaliatory missile barrages on Ukraine, the repeated strikes on the Crimea bridge, and the missile landing in Poland made aerial and missile warfare the central military story.

delta.motion: Between the two photographs, the dominant shift is from a week defined by diplomatic anticipation to one defined by diplomatic performance and military escalation in parallel. The Shenzhen summit, which in the first photograph was an announced future event, became in the second the single anchoring story, producing a joint 'Declaration toward Peace,' a photo op with Putin's nuclear briefcase in the room, and a visible snub to Europe. The theme that grew most dramatically was the 'war of bridges': Ukraine's repeated strikes on the Kerch Bridge, partially collapsing a section, and Russia's vow of a 'far more painful' response, turned infrastructure targeting into a symbolic and strategic contest that was not a named theme in the first photograph. Russian missile and drone barrages on Ukraine escalated from 'expected continuation' to some of the war's largest waves, including a triple-tap strike that killed a seven-year-old in Zelensky's hometown, which is a step up in both scale and human drama. The Baltic and Northern European front grew from scattered incidents (a warship hit, a data-center drone attack) into a coordinated hotspot: a cargo ship hit in the Gulf of Finland, a helicopter near Finnish airspace, a foiled assassination plot in Denmark, Estonia announcing it will close its land border on December 1, and a Russian missile landing in Polish territory during NATO exercises. This is a new cluster of events that was only hinted at in the first photograph. Russia's energy strain grew from 'refineries being hit' to 'November refining capacity nearly halved, record petrol imports, multiple regions rationing fuel,' which is a materially worse picture. Russia's Asian repositioning, which in the first photograph was an upcoming summit, became an explicit declaration: Putin calling Russia an 'integral part of Asia-Pacific,' nuclear-capable bombers spotted in Vietnam, and energy deals with Vietnam. The EU's role grew from internal squabbling over who to send to concrete actions: sanctioning Wildberries' CEO, proposing a 45-billion-euro loan to Ukraine, and a visa ban for former Russian combatants. What shrank or vanished: the prisoner exchange, expected to be a headline, is barely visible in the second photograph; the specific car-bombing narrative in Moscow fades; the bear population, the Madagascar story, the 'beer-loving nations alliance,' and the Novaya Gazeta closure are no longer active threads. The sports dispute did not shrink but intensified: Russia was formally barred from the World Junior Hockey tournament, the IIHF website was hacked, and Putin personally criticized the ruling. New domestic stories appeared: a military transport plane crash in Siberia killing 19, a WSJ investigation into sex abuse in a POW camp, and a renowned ornithologist jailed over small donations to Navalny's foundation. The espionage thread continued but shifted focus: a Russian national was charged by the US DOJ for targeting Palantir, and the UK Army officer case moved from arrest to formal custody. Overall, the motion is from anticipation and setup to performance and escalation: the diplomatic stage was set, the military stakes were raised, and the geographic footprint of the conflict widened northward and eastward.
delta.wind: The expectation that the Shenzhen summit would happen, produce a joint statement, and be more about positioning than substance was broadly correct. The summit happened, produced the 'Declaration toward Peace,' and Trump himself said nuclear arms limits would be 'very hard to achieve,' confirming the positioning-over-substance read. The Yalta comparisons materialized, and the European snub was exactly as predicted. The one miss was the prisoner exchange, which was expected to be a probable headline event between November 15 and 21; it does not appear as a major story in the second photograph, suggesting it either happened quietly, slipped, or was overshadowed by the summit and the bridge strikes. The expectation of continued drone strikes on Russian infrastructure was correct, but the form was different: the strikes were not just on refineries and ports but concentrated on the Kerch Bridge, creating a new 'war of bridges' theme that was not in the forecast. The expectation of 'probable that at least one major Russian refinery or port is hit again' was met, but the bridge was a more symbolic and strategically significant target than was anticipated. The EU sanctions package was expected to be adopted on November 17, and while the adoption itself is not the headline in the second photograph, the EU's subsequent actions (sanctioning Wildberries' CEO, the 45-billion-euro loan, the visa ban) show the sanctions track continued and evolved, which is consistent with the expectation but more specific than predicted. The expectation that Europe would finalize its delegation was partly met: the EU declared itself ready for talks, but the Kallas question became a point of contention rather than a clean resolution, and Russia said Kallas's involvement would lead to collapse. The expectation of 'possible one more targeted incident' domestically was met in a different form: the military transport plane crash in Siberia is more of an accident than a targeted strike, but it fits the pattern of domestic incidents. The oil and diesel expectation of 'continued volatility' was an understatement: the halving of November refining capacity and record petrol imports are a more severe deterioration than 'volatility' implies. The sports dispute expectation of 'probable the dispute continues' was correct but understated: the formal barring from the World Juniors, the website hack, and Putin's personal criticism pushed the dispute to a more heated level. The nuclear arms expectation of 'probable a statement, possible a framework, unlikely a signed treaty' was accurate: the joint declaration exists, no framework or treaty was signed, and Trump's 'very hard to achieve' remark confirms the gap. What was not expected and came: the Poland missile incident (listed as a less-likely surprise, but a missile in Polish territory during NATO exercises is more dramatic than a cyberattack on infrastructure); the Denmark assassination plot and Estonia border closure, which together form a new Baltic escalation cluster; the 'triple-tap' attack and the killing of a seven-year-old, which raised the human stakes beyond the 'dozens dead or missing' that was implied; Russia's explicit 'integral part of Asia-Pacific' declaration and the bombers in Vietnam, which made the Asian pivot from a sub-plot to a declared strategy; the 45-billion-euro EU loan and the visa ban for former combatants, which are concrete EU measures that go beyond the sanctions package that was forecast; and the WSJ POW camp investigation, which is a new domestic accountability story. What this says about the way expectations have been wrong for Russia: the forecast was structurally sound on the diplomatic track but underweighted the military escalation and the geographic widening of the conflict. The expectation treated the summit as the anchor and everything else as supporting cast, but in reality the bridge strikes and the Baltic incidents were co-equal stories. The expectation was too optimistic about the prisoner exchange being a visible headline and too conservative about the energy damage (halving of refining capacity is a step beyond 'volatility'). The expectation also underweighted Russia's deliberate Asian repositioning as a stated policy rather than a tactical move, and it did not anticipate the specific form of European coordination (Berlin meeting, loan, visa ban) that emerged as a package. The overall pattern is that the expectations captured the right themes but the wrong intensity and the wrong specific targets, and they treated the diplomatic and military tracks as sequential (summit first, then military) when in reality they ran in parallel and fed each other.
delta.driver: The force pushing Russia from the first photograph to the second is the collision between a great-power diplomatic performance and a war that is simultaneously intensifying and widening geographically. Russia is using the Shenzhen summit to lock in its status as one of three co-equal powers, to signal to Europe that the big decisions are being made without them, and to anchor its pivot toward Asia as a declared strategic direction rather than a fallback. At the same time, the military campaign is escalating in both intensity and symbolism: the Kerch Bridge strikes represent a new phase in which both sides target not just capacity but the physical and psychological links that hold territories together, and the triple-tap barrage in Kryvyi Rih is a message that the war is still very much a war of attrition with human cost. The Baltic and Polish incidents show that the shadow war is no longer a sub-plot but a parallel front, with Russia testing European nerves through airspace violations, sabotage plots, and a missile in Polish territory during NATO exercises, all of which raise the question of whether a miscalculation could become a trigger. Domestically, the halving of refining capacity, record fuel imports, and the transport plane crash are creating a pressure to either accelerate the diplomatic track or absorb the cost of a longer war. The underlying driver is therefore a three-way tension: Russia wants to be seen as a great power negotiating from strength, it needs to keep military pressure high enough to hold its leverage in the talks, and it must manage the domestic and economic costs of a war that is increasingly hitting its own soil, its own fuel supply, and its own symbolic infrastructure. The Asian pivot is the long-term hedge, the bridge war is the short-term lever, and the Baltic incidents are the pressure test for whether Europe will stay at the table or be pushed to the sidelines.

crystal.reasoning:
Starting from the present: Russia enters this week as the self-declared 'integral part of Asia-Pacific,' fresh from a trilateral photo op in Shenzhen that produced a 'Declaration toward Peace' but no substance, while its Kerch Bridge lies partially collapsed, its November refining capacity is nearly halved, a missile has just landed in Polish territory during NATO exercises, and a seven-year-old has been killed in a triple-tap strike in Zelensky's hometown. The motion from the previous week was a shift from anticipation to performance and escalation: the diplomatic stage was set, the military stakes were raised, and the geographic footprint widened northward into the Baltics and eastward into Southeast Asia. The wind tells me my expectations have been structurally sound but consistently too gentle on intensity, too sequential in treating diplomacy and war as separate tracks when they run in parallel, and too conservative on the specific form of escalation (the 'war of bridges' was not anticipated as a named category; the Baltic cluster was treated as a sub-plot when it is now a parallel front). The prisoner exchange was over-weighted; the energy damage was under-weighted; the Asian pivot was treated as tactical when it is now declared policy.

Extending each theme along its motion: The post-summit week will be about managing the gap between the 'Declaration toward Peace' and the reality of no breakthroughs. Russia will try to bank the summit's goodwill while maintaining a hard negotiating posture. The Kallas question and the NATO-guarantee dispute need resolution before any substantive talks can proceed, so expect diplomatic sparring and possibly a second round of back-channel contacts. The EU's Berlin coordination will produce concrete follow-up measures: the 45-billion-euro loan will move toward a vote, the visa ban for former combatants will be formalized, and the Wildberries CEO departure will be followed by additional corporate sanctions.

The war of bridges is the defining military theme. Putin has vowed a 'far more painful' response, and the pattern of mutual infrastructure targeting will continue. Ukraine will likely strike more Russian transport links, possibly targeting other bridges or rail corridors, while Russia will hit Ukrainian river crossings and energy nodes. The 'flying modems' technology gives Ukraine a new precision edge that Russia must account for. Expect at least one high-casualty barrage, possibly another triple-tap, and continued targeting of energy facilities as winter deepens.

The Baltic and Northern European shadow war is now an established front, not a sub-plot. Estonia's December 1 border closure is a hard date ten days away and will generate a final wave of diplomatic friction. The Polish missile incident during NATO exercises will trigger formal consultations and possibly a military response or a new round of airspace patrols. The Danish assassination plot and Finnish helicopter incident suggest a coordinated or at least parallel Russian pressure campaign in the region. I expect at least one more Baltic/Northern incident, possibly a maritime event in the Gulf of Finland or another airspace violation.

The energy crisis is the quiet domestic story that is getting louder. With November refining capacity nearly halved, record petrol imports, and multiple regions rationing, the pain is becoming visible in gas station queues, regional price announcements, and the Defense Ministry's logistics. The Tatarstan oil facility hit and the broader drone campaign against refineries mean the situation is likely to worsen before it improves. Expect more regional rationing announcements, possibly a federal-level response, and continued friction over the diesel deal.

The Asian pivot is now declared policy, not a fallback. Vietnam energy cooperation, nuclear-capable bombers spotted in Vietnam, and Putin's explicit 'integral part of Asia-Pacific' language suggest Russia is building a second axis of engagement. Expect more Asian diplomatic or economic activity in the coming week, possibly a specific energy deal or a military-technical announcement.

Correcting for the wind: I am weighting the military escalation more heavily than I did last week, treating the diplomatic and military tracks as parallel rather than sequential, expecting the Baltic front to produce at least one concrete incident, and treating the energy crisis as a worsening condition rather than a stable one. I am also giving more weight to the Asian pivot as a source of specific news events rather than background context. The less-likely surprises the motion makes more likely include: a second or third major infrastructure strike on the Kerch Bridge or a parallel target; a dramatic Russian military response in the Baltic (not just a missile in Poland but a visible fleet movement or a second airspace violation); a specific fuel-crisis event in a named Russian region; and a concrete Asian deal or military-technical announcement. What I would not bet on: a signed ceasefire or peace framework; a major Russian ground offensive; Putin making a surprise visit to Europe or the US; a full nuclear arms framework; a mass Moscow street protest; or the Kerch Bridge being fully repaired within the week.

crystal.headline: Russia Vows Painful Response as Bridge War and Baltic Tensions Escalate
emoji_reasons: The post-Shenzhen diplomatic week and Russia's declared Asian pivot are the dominant diplomatic thread of the coming week.
The war of bridges, massive missile and drone barrages, and the expanding Baltic shadow war define the military escalation.

crystal.tldr: Russia enters the week managing the gap between its triumphant Shenzhen photo op and the reality of no breakthroughs, while the war of bridges, Baltic shadow incidents, and a deepening fuel crisis all escalate in parallel. crystal.eli5:
Think of it like this: Russia just had a really fancy photo shoot with the US and China leaders, where everyone shook hands and smiled for the cameras. But when you look at what they actually agreed on, it was mostly 'we'll keep talking' and no real plan. So next week, everyone is going to be talking about that photo shoot, and Europe is going to be a little miffed because it wasn't invited to the party.

At the same time, the actual fighting is getting more intense. Ukraine knocked a big bridge that connects Russia to Crimea, and now both sides are hitting each other's bridges, roads, and power plants. Russia promised to hit back harder, and it's probably going to do that with big missile attacks. Up in the Baltic region, where Russia borders countries like Poland, Finland, and Denmark, there's been a whole string of scary incidents: a missile landed in Poland, a ship got hit, and Denmark found out Russia was planning to kill a celebrity. All of that is happening at the same time, which makes it feel like the fight is spreading.

And at home in Russia, the fuel situation is getting rough. The factories that make gasoline and diesel are getting bombed, so there's less fuel to go around. Some regions are already rationing, and people are probably going to start noticing longer lines at gas stations and higher prices. It's like a car where the gas tank is leaking and you're trying to drive to a really important meeting. The diplomatic meeting is the shiny part, but the leaking tank is the part that's going to hurt in the long run.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A was broadly accurate on the major themes of the week.
